children.text: Realtime Audio Metamorphosis (RAM) is a game made in Unreal Engine. You fly a butterfly with no memory through a post-human landscape, collecting swarms that rebuild a soundtrack and finding flowers that keep you alive.

alt: a metallic butterfly flying through a dark landscape, with a swarm of small glowing butterflies around it

children.text: Environment and visuals: the butterfly and cave in Blender, the Niagara butterfly swarms, procedural materials, lighting and volumetric fog in Unreal.
2025. Final project for CART 498 at Concordia.
Unreal Engine (MetaSounds, Niagara, Blueprints, AnimToTexture), Blender. Development build for Windows.
the concept
RAM is set in a world after people, where today's hardware (motherboards, cables, brutalist concrete) has become the landscape. It reads as ancient and hard to make sense of, the way old ruins do.

You play a small organism with no long-term memory, driven only by what it senses right now. The game is built around hide and seek: what you need to survive is hidden, and if you can't find it in time your memory fails and you start again.
how it plays
Sonic Swarms are clusters of butterflies, each holding one part of the music. Fly through one and it follows you, adding a permanent layer to the soundtrack.
Your memory drains constantly. Hover near a glowing Neon Flower to recharge it. Flowers without a glow are used up and give nothing.
If your memory runs out, you die and the level resets.
controls
W A S D:
move forward, left, back and right.
mouse:
pitch and altitude. Look up or down to fly up or down.
left shift:
sprint.
key decisions
1. synthesise the music live
problem.
the soundtrack had to react to the player's state, and a fixed recording can't do that.
options.
pre-recorded loops, or live synthesis.
decision.

the whole soundscape is synthesised in real time in MetaSounds, from oscillators and noise generators instead of samples. Note patterns are generated as the game runs, so each playthrough sounds different.
trade-off.
a live mix is harder to balance than a recorded one. The overall mix is still on the list to refine.

alt: the MetaSound source graph in Unreal, with oscillators and generators feeding the soundtrack
caption: MetaSounds: the soundtrack is generated in real time

children.text: 2. make the soundtrack the progress
problem.
the player needs a reason to explore, and a sense of how far they've got.
decision.

the background music is split into six parts (melody, bass, kick, hi-hat, beep and boop), and each one is a swarm hidden somewhere in the map. Collecting them rebuilds the full arrangement, so progress is something you hear.
trade-off.
the swarms are in the same places every time. Random placement is planned.
3. show health through sound and image, not a bar
problem.
a health bar pulls attention to the corner of the screen and away from the world.
decision.

health drains over time. As it falls, the tempo slows, the note patterns change and the pitch detunes, and a datamosh effect builds up until the screen is hard to read. Finding a flower brings it all back.
trade-off.
with no on-screen meter, new players need more guidance. In-game cues and a tutorial are planned.

alt: the health component Blueprint in Unreal
caption: the health component: decay drives tempo, pitch and the datamosh effect

children.text: 4. a butterfly made of metal and muscle
problem.
the main character needed to look organic and machine-made at once, and still animate cheaply.
decision.

two meshes joined together: a standard butterfly body, and wings subdivided several times and run through wireframe and solidify modifiers, then cleaned up into a metallic, muscle-like surface. Each wing is rigged with one bone (two per side). The flap plays twice as fast when the butterfly moves forward, blended with Unreal blend spaces.

images.alt: an early version of the butterfly standing in a rocky cave
close-up of the final wing mesh: a web of metallic strands

caption: early version and final wing mesh

children.text: 5. swarms as particles
problem.
each Sonic Swarm needed many animated butterflies, but Niagara particle systems can't use skeletal meshes or their animations.
decision.

a simpler butterfly from an early version, sharing the main butterfly's skeleton and animation at different angles and speeds. AnimToTexture, a built-in Unreal tool, bakes that animation into vertex animation on a static mesh, which Niagara can use as particles.
6. a cave that Unreal could handle
problem.
the first cave, modelled in Blender with a displacement modifier, came out as overlapping meshes with very complex UVs, which looked wrong in Unreal.
options.
fix the Blender mesh, or move displacement into Unreal.
decision.
a simpler base mesh from Blender, displaced in Unreal. The UVs were still hard to manage on something that large, so the surfaces use simple procedural materials that don't depend on UVs.
trade-off.
less hand control over how the texture sits on the surface.

images.alt: the cave mesh in Unreal's modelling tools, highlighted in blue
the procedural material node graph for the cave

caption: the cave in Unreal and its procedural material

children.text: outcome

What worked: procedural sound generation, the reactive tempo and real-time effects, the flying system, the Niagara swarms, the cave, local and global lighting with volumetric fog, and the flower recharge and depletion system.
next
In-game tutorials or visual cues to explain the mechanics and guide players.
Refine the overall mix.
Let the butterfly land and walk as well as fly.
Randomise where swarms and flowers appear on each playthrough.
Spatial audio, so players can find sounds by ear.
One-shot sounds for healing and death.
More detailed collisions.
